transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-05-22 15:00 PT
Duration: 55 minutes approx
Attendees: Anika (Redwood AE), Marco (Redwood SE), Lisa (Seastar CISO), Omar (Head Research), Priya (Ops), Ravi (Legal)

Auto-generated summary: (may be imperfect) Seastar wants confirmation that data wont be used to train models, KMS is available, and logs/audit meet their SOX and PCI style needs, mostly healthcare oriented.

[00:00] Anika: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — I see Lisa, Omar, Priya, Ravi — can you hear me okay?
[00:08] Lisa: Yep, loud and clear.
[00:10] Omar: yes thanks.
[00:12] Priya: all good.
[00:14] Anika: Great. The goal for today is to walk through Redwood's security posture focused on data residency, encryption/KMS options, and specifically the no‑train / prompt retention commitments. Marco will jump into some of the technical bits.
[00:30] Marco: Hey team — I'll start with a high-level on our compliance stack. Redwood has a SOC 2 Type II attestation, we also maintain an ISO 27001 alignment package, uh, and we publish the scoping doc. I should say up front some of the artifacts are redacted when we share them.
[00:46] Lisa: Can you be explicit, like, will the SOC 2 cover the hosted API environment and the dedicated deployments? We run some workloads that might go to dedicated pools.
[00:58] Marco: Yeah good question. SOC 2 covers our hosted control plane and the hosted inference clusters. For Dedicated — the reserved capacity product — we have contractual SLAs and isolation controls; we also provide a separate addendum for dedicated contracts that maps controls. I'll attach the dedicated addendum.
[01:16] Ravi: Is there an ISO certificate we can reference? We are 2nd party audited and ISO alignment matters for our vendor onboarding.
[01:24] Marco: We have an ISO 27001 alignment report, it's not yet fully certified at the time of this call — roadmap item — but we can share the current statement of applicability and our implementation plan.
[01:36] Lisa: Ok. Next KMS — we need to see customer‑managed keys, please. Any options for HSM?
[01:44] Anika: Short answer: yes. We support both Redwood‑managed KMS and customer‑managed KMS through integrations with AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and external HSMs via KMIP in private deployments. For hosted customers we can do customer‑managed keys through an account level KMS integration.
[02:04] Omar: Does that mean we can rotate keys and Redwood won't have plaintext access?
[02:09] Marco: Correct — with customer‑managed keys in KMS, our services store only encrypted model inputs/outputs and ephemeral caches using keys you control. The key policy can prevent the Redwood service principal from decrypt permissions if you require that — there's a configured flow for service wrap keys and re‑encryption for runtime. There is a small caveat: for certain optimizations we keep transient in‑memory plaintext on the GPU nodes during inference, but it's never written to disk and it's scoped to the request lifecycle.
[02:40] Priya: That in‑memory note — we need an architecture diagram for that flow, like when data is loaded, decrypted, used, and purged.
[02:46] Marco: Absolutely, I'll include that.
[02:50] Lisa: Audit logs — we need full request trail: who called the API, token id, model used, region, and raw request metadata. Also retention of logs for 2 years for compliance and searchability.
[03:04] Marco: We emit detailed audit logs to a tenant log stream; for hosted we can push to your cloud log ingestion, or provide a managed retention option. Default retention is 90 days; we can extend to 2 years under enterprise plan. Logs include request identifiers, token hash, model id, latency, region, but raw request body is masked by default.
[03:24] Ravi: Masked — is that configurable? For some of our legal signoffs, we need the ability to retain request bodies in an encrypted form.
[03:32] Marco: We can offer configurable retention where request bodies are archived encrypted with your KMS, but that is an opt‑in enterprise feature. We'll need to discuss retention class and the storage location (region).
[03:44] Lisa: Data residency — we must keep EU patient data in EU. Can you pin inference to eu‑west‑3 and ensure logs and keys stay in region?
[03:52] Marco: Yes, we support region pinning for inference. For hosted we have EU regions and you can request region locking for both inference and log egress. For keys, if you bring your KMS in the EU, the keys remain in the region. For Dedicated VPC/on‑prem, it's straightforward since it's in your network.
[04:10] Priya: If we route traffic from our EU VPC to Redwood hosted EU region, is there any cross‑border failover that might send data to us‑west?
[04:18] Marco: Not unless you enable cross‑region failover. We do have failover policies, but for customers with residency concerns, we set strict routing policies — no cross‑border failover — and provide a fallback model in the same region.
[04:32] Omar: About prompt retention and training — we've seen other vendors claim they don't train, but then their terms allow it. We need contractual no‑train language and technical isolation assurances.
[04:44] Anika: Understood. Redwood's standard position: for enterprise customers, we offer a 'no training on customer data' contractual clause and we configure your tenant to opt out of any training telemetry. That includes not persisting prompts to our training datasets and no aggregation for model updates.
[05:00] Ravi: Can we get an explicit attestation — legal language we can put in our agreement?
[05:04] Anika: Yes, we'll provide an attestation letter. I'll get Legal to produce the exact language. It will state we do not use customer prompts or outputs for model training, and the clause will include exceptions if any — e.g., explicit opt‑in — which you can disable.
[05:20] Lisa: Are there any telemetry signals we still collect for product/security monitoring that could leak PII?
[05:28] Marco: We collect standard telemetry (error rates, latency, sampling of request metadata). By default request bodies are not stored; if you enable body retention it's archived encrypted with your KMS. For PII/PHI, we recommend tokenization at your side or the use of our redaction pipeline — we also offer a PII scrubber pre‑ingest which can be enforced in the tenant.
[05:50] Omar: The scrubber — is it deterministic? We need reproducible results for audit.
[05:55] Marco: The scrubber applies deterministic rules and ML heuristics; we'll share the rulebook and an evaluation. It's configurable and can be run client‑side as well.
[06:05] Priya: On RBAC and SSO: we use Okta and SCIM for provisioning. How does Redwood integrate?
[06:12] Anika: We support SAML 2.0 SSO, SCIM provisioning, and role‑based policies (admin, engineer, reader). We also have per‑token scopes for API keys and session tokens, and audit trails for every token issuance.
[06:28] Lisa: For emergency access, can we lock down support access unless there is a signed escalation? We need break‑glass controls.
[06:36] Marco: Yes, we have break‑glass workflows that require SSO re‑auth and customer approval for support sessions. All support sessions are logged and recorded in the audit log.
[06:46] Ravi: Have you undergone penetration tests and will you share the executive summary?
[06:50] Marco: We run regular 3rd‑party pen tests annually. We can share the exec summary and remediation timeline; full reports are redacted but available under NDA.
[07:02] Lisa: Ok, pivoting back to the no‑train attestation — how is it enforced technically? Is there a tenant flag?
[07:10] Marco: There's a tenant configuration flag that turns off training telemetry emission. When enabled, live requests still flow for inference but we do not copy them to training stores. For extra assurance we can enable access controls so that training pipelines do not have read access to tenant buckets or log archives by default.
[07:28] Omar: Is there any aggregation of anonymized signals used for modeling?
[07:32] Marco: We sometimes use aggregate telemetry like latency histograms and token frequency distributions, but not request level or content-level aggregates for customers with no‑train enabled. We can also disable even the aggregate collection if required.
[07:46] Priya: For the pilot, we want to test with our EU dataset and customer KMS. Can Marco outline the pilot steps?
[07:54] Marco: Sure — step 1: we provision a tenant in eu‑west‑3 and connect to your KMS key; step 2: we configure region lock and no‑train flag; step 3: run a set of benchmark scripts (we'll provide a harness) and capture latency, throughput, and audit logs. We'll also validate that audit logs are exported to your log collector.
[08:18] Anika: We'll include the legal attestation and SOC artifacts with the pilot materials.
[08:24] Ravi: Regarding documentation — we need sample contract language for the no‑train clause and an example of the KMS integration appendix.
[08:30] Anika: I'll attach both. Legal will send the attestation and the KMS appendix.
[08:36] Lisa: One last question — do you ever use customer data for model evaluation (Evals) for quality checks?
[08:44] Marco: Not by default. For our eval processes, we only use synthetic tests or customer redacted datasets if customers opt in and provide explicit written consent. For Seastar with no‑train enabled, we will not use any of your prompts or outputs in evals.
[08:58] Omar: Good. Any SLA on data deletion after contract termination? We want guaranteed purge within 30 days and certificate of deletion.
[09:06] Marco: Standard enterprise terms allow for configurable deletion windows. We can commit to 30 days and provide a deletion certificate. That will be added to the contract addendum.
[09:18] Priya: Perfect.
[09:20] Anika: Let's recap next steps — I'll send SOC 2 summary, legal attestation no‑train, KMS appendix, and schedule Marco's pilot run. Ravi, you'll review attestation language; Priya will send dataset/residency list. Any other asks?
[09:36] Ravi: No, that's it.
[09:38] Lisa: Thanks everyone.
[09:40] Anika: Thanks — we'll follow up in email.

(Transcript notes: occasional speaker mislabels present in auto‑transcript; some technical terms spelled phonetically. Phrases like 'no train' sometimes appear as 'no‑trane' in sections.)
